rules.descriptionEn: Curcumin may potentiate warfarin’s anticoagulant effect, increasing bleeding risk (bruising, gum bleeding, dark stools).
rules.adviceEn: Consult your prescribing physician before combining high-dose turmeric supplements with blood thinners; do not stop warfarin on your own.

rules.descriptionEn: Turmeric has mild antiplatelet activity that may add to aspirin’s effect and increase bleeding tendency.
rules.adviceEn: Prefer culinary turmeric; discuss any turmeric/curcumin supplement with your physician first.

rules.descriptionEn: Additive antiplatelet effect may raise bleeding risk when curcumin supplements are combined with clopidogrel.
rules.adviceEn: Inform your cardiologist about all herbal supplements before stent procedures or antiplatelet therapy.

rules.descriptionEn: Ashwagandha may add to sedative effects — increased drowsiness, impaired alertness, and falls risk in elderly.
rules.adviceEn: Avoid driving after combining; ask your physician whether dose adjustment is needed.

rules.descriptionEn: Ashwagandha can increase thyroid hormone levels; combined with levothyroxine it may cause symptoms of excess thyroid hormone.
rules.adviceEn: Monitor TSH after starting; consult your endocrinologist before combining.
sources: Case reports of thyrotoxicosis with ashwagandha (PubMed-indexed)

rules.descriptionEn: Immunostimulatory activity of ashwagandha may theoretically counteract immunosuppressive therapy.
rules.adviceEn: Avoid ashwagandha if you are on transplant or autoimmune immunosuppression unless your specialist approves.

rules.descriptionEn: Garlic supplements (not culinary amounts) may add to warfarin’s effect and raise INR/bleeding risk.
rules.adviceEn: Keep culinary garlic; avoid concentrated supplements without physician approval; check INR as advised.

rules.descriptionEn: Garlic has mild antiplatelet activity that can add to aspirin, especially with supplements at high doses.
rules.adviceEn: Stop garlic supplements 1–2 weeks before planned surgery (with your surgeon’s knowledge).

rules.descriptionEn: Fenugreek lowers glucose by its own mechanism; combined with metformin, hypoglycaemia is possible though uncommon.
rules.adviceEn: Monitor fasting glucose when starting fenugreek; carry fast-acting glucose; inform your diabetologist.

rules.descriptionEn: Additive glucose-lowering with insulin may increase hypoglycaemia risk as fenugreek takes effect over weeks.
rules.adviceEn: Do not change insulin doses yourself; track glucose logs and review with your diabetologist.

rules.descriptionEn: Cinnamon may add a mild glucose-lowering effect; clinically significant hypoglycaemia is uncommon but possible.
rules.adviceEn: Prefer Ceylon cinnamon in food amounts; monitor glucose when starting supplements.
sources: Meta-analyses of cinnamon on glycaemic control (2022)

rules.descriptionEn: Glycyrrhizin causes sodium retention and potassium loss, raising blood pressure and counteracting antihypertensive drugs.
rules.adviceEn: Avoid whole-licorice (mulethi) use if you have hypertension; DGL forms are the safer alternative — confirm with your physician.
sources: EU Scientific Committee on Food glycyrrhizin guidance

rules.descriptionEn: Combined potassium loss (licorice + loop/thiazide diuretics) can cause dangerous hypokalaemia and arrhythmia risk.
rules.adviceEn: Avoid licorice entirely on diuretics; check serum potassium if accidental combined use occurred.

rules.descriptionEn: Guduchi may add to glucose-lowering; combined hypoglycaemia is possible.
rules.adviceEn: Monitor glucose during first weeks; inform your diabetologist before starting.

rules.descriptionEn: Guduchi is immunostimulatory and may theoretically counteract immunosuppressive therapy; rare liver injury reports exist with prolonged use.
rules.adviceEn: Avoid in transplant/autoimmune immunosuppression; keep any use short and physician-supervised.
sources: Case reports of autoimmune hepatitis with Tinospora (PubMed-indexed)

rules.descriptionEn: Neem preparations may lower glucose; additive effect with metformin can cause hypoglycaemia.
rules.adviceEn: Use neem only short-term and physician-supervised; monitor glucose closely.

rules.descriptionEn: Tulsi shows mild antiplatelet activity in preclinical work; additive effect with aspirin is possible but usually not clinically significant.
rules.adviceEn: Tea amounts are fine; mention tulsi supplements if you have a bleeding disorder.
sources: Preclinical platelet studies of Ocimum sanctum (PubMed-indexed)

rules.descriptionEn: Brahmi may add mild drowsiness to sedative medication.
rules.adviceEn: Take with food; observe response before driving or machine work.
sources: Clinical trial safety summaries for Bacopa (PubMed-indexed)

rules.descriptionEn: Culinary ginger is generally safe; large doses (>4 g/day) may add to anticoagulant effect.
rules.adviceEn: Keep doses culinary; avoid concentrated supplements while on warfarin without medical advice.

rules.descriptionEn: Theoretical additive antiplatelet effect at high supplement doses; culinary use is fine.
rules.adviceEn: Prefer whole fruit; avoid high-dose amla supplements on anticoagulants.
